title: The Paraguay missions
hookLine: Jesuits and Guaraní peoples built towns together, which colonial powers later ended

cards: Red sandstone walls stand roofless on a green hill in southern Paraguay. Carved angels play instruments along a frieze, one of them a harp. Grass grows where the floor was.
This was once a town's church, with a plaza, rows of houses, workshops, a school, fields around it. The people who built and lived in it were Guaraní. The priests who lived among them were Jesuits.
Then the towns were emptied, and the forest came back.

teach.b: The Spanish called these towns reducciones, reductions, meaning people gathered together into a settlement. First, the shelter.

Colonists wanted Guaraní labor, and slave raiders came from the Portuguese side to carry people off. The Jesuits gathered Guaraní families into towns under the Spanish crown, where settlers had no claim on their work.
At one point the Guaraní were even allowed to carry arms to defend themselves. Second, the language. The Jesuits learned Guaraní instead of replacing it.
They preached in it, wrote grammars, and printed books in it. Third, the music and the work.
The towns had workshops, fields held in common, choirs and orchestras. Guaraní craftsmen built instruments and played European music in the forest.
Acts describes the first believers, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul." Fourth, the end.

teach.h: A BORDER, A WAR, AN EXPULSION.
teach.b: Spain and Portugal redrew their border and ordered Guaraní towns handed over. The Guaraní resisted and were defeated in war. Then the Spanish king expelled the Jesuits from his lands, and the towns slowly emptied.
People still argue about the missions.
Some see a refuge that protected a people and their language. Others see priests who, however kind, ran the Guaraní's lives for them. The two readings don't cancel each other out.
What the stones themselves show is the work of Guaraní builders and carvers, whose hands cut those walls and many of those angels.

how: Catholics in Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil visit the mission ruins as pilgrims and tourists, and some parishes there still sing and play music from the mission tradition.

practice: Look at your own hands for a moment, then think of the hands that cut that red stone and carved those angels. Bring to mind Guaraní families today, in Paraguay and its neighbors, speaking a language their ancestors kept alive.
If you pray, pray for them, their land and their children; if you don't, hold them in mind with respect.

wordCard.voice: Reducción. The Spanish word for a settlement where Guaraní families were gathered together, under Jesuit priests, sheltered from slave raiders.

orig.note: Spanish: a reduction, a settlement where people were gathered together into one town.

carryVoice: Your line: the reductions. The red stone still stands where the towns once were. Day eight hundred eighty-four.
